title: You Have Been Wrong About Your Limits
author: Stoic Wisdoms
summary: The argument here is that your self-assessment is structurally out of date, and that this is a measurement problem rather than a confidence problem. The governing image is the pencil mark on a doorframe: no child feels themselves grow, and strength works the same way except nobody draws the lines, so once a burden stops feeling heavy the mind stops counting it. The consequence is that the person whose limits you consult before every decision is a version of you from several marks ago. Seneca supplies the corollary, that an untested life leaves you a stranger to your own powers, and Epictetus supplies the replacement question, since asking whether you can handle this demands a measurement only available afterwards. The essay then handles the objection about pace with Cleanthes, the slow student the others called the donkey, who wrote on oyster shells because he could not afford papyrus and inherited Zeno's school after nineteen years. From there it lands on the Stoic self-description of prokopton, one making progress, and on Hecato's single-sentence answer that his progress was beginning to be a friend to himself. The practical close is a ten-minute writing exercise for keeping your own doorframe.
points: Frames the core error as a missing measurement rather than weak character, since strength becomes invisible the moment it becomes sufficient.
Recasts the three-in-the-morning question as unanswerable by definition, and substitutes the Epictetus question about which faculty the situation calls for.
Uses Cleanthes to dismantle the comparison with faster people, noting the school passed to the slow student rather than the quick ones.
Offers prokopton as the most any Stoic claimed to be, removing the imagined finished group a reader is failing to join.
Ends with a concrete exercise: write down three things you believed you could not survive, what you feared, and what actually happened.
quotes: It did not get smaller. You got bigger. And the trouble with getting bigger is that you can’t feel it happen.
Strength grows the same way, except nobody draws the lines. Once you can carry something it stops feeling heavy, and once it stops feeling heavy your mind stops counting it.
This leaves you with a picture of yourself that is always out of date. The person whose limits you consult before every decision is the person from several lines ago.
The Stoics believed a human being comes equipped for a human life, and that the equipment shows itself when it is called for and not a minute before.
If strength arrives on demand, then waiting until you feel strong enough means waiting for something that only comes after you begin.
Cleanthes never entered the comparison with the quick students, because he could not win it and it measured nothing he cared about.
A friend is the person who remembers what you have come through when you have forgotten it, who keeps the doorframe on your behalf.
